item.title: SALES: The 7 Best Hiking Boots for Weak Ankles in 2026
item.description:
Source: Backpacker Magazine
If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy Hiking boots have lost some ground to trail runners and low-cut shoes over the past decade, but don’t write them off just yet: If you have weak ankles or are prone to stumbles, an old-school hiking boot may be exactly what you need, especially if your trips often involve rough terrain or heavier loads. Besides providing protection from rolls and twists, a mid-cut boot can help lower your injury risk by supporting your foot and ankle and easing the fatigue and soreness that builds up over the course of a long backpacking trip. We’ve gone through our favorite hiking boots of 2026 and picked our seven faves for hikers with problem ankles, four from our men’s list and three from our women’s roundup, both curated by Blair Braverman, the expert reviewer at our sibling site Backpacker. Our picks run the gamut from super-supportive leather lace-ups to lightweight mid-cuts with a sneaker-like feel. All earned our testers’ approval over hundreds of trail miles, so you can confidently buy the best hiking boot for your weak ankles. Weight: 16.9 oz (men’s) / 13.4 oz (women’s) Sizes: Men’s 37-47.5 (EU) / Women’s 36-42 (EU) If you want the best hiking boot for weak ankles that money can buy this year—no matter how much money it costs—this is it. While it’s designed for three-season alpine use, we found it a perfect tool for rugged backpacking trips, thanks to a durable PU midsole with a polypropylene stiffener, a “bouncy and cushioned” PU-injected rubber outsole, and a reinforced toe and heel that looked “pristine” after more than 100 often-rough miles on the trail. Read the full review. Weight: 20.1 oz (men’s) / 16.6 oz (women’s) If you love an old-school hiker, the Keen Targhee IV Waterproof Mid is the hiking boot for you. This generously cushioned leather mid-cut shrugged off scrapes from rocks and comes with a lifetime guarantee against delamination of the sole. Its bulletproof waterproofing made it perfectly suited for wet, sloppy trail. Read the full review. Weight: 12 oz (men’s) / 11 oz (women’s) One pound on your feet burns as much energy as three pounds in your pack, so we’d call this lightweight mid-cut hiking boot a calorie-saver. The Arc’teryx Kopec Mid GTX is a perfect do-anything boot, as comfortable on high-tempo day hikes as it is toting a pack with a week of supplies, but still wards off foot and ankle fatigue with its supportive midsole. Read the full review. Weight: 14.5 oz (men’s) / 11.5 oz (women’s) Sometimes, your pack is just going to be heavy—think supply-intensive deep wilderness trips or family outings where you end up carrying other people’s gear. The Danner N45 Mid GTX hiking boot feels tailor-made for those missions, especially if you have weak ankles, with bouncy nitrogen-infused foam in the midsole, a TPU rock plate, and a breathable nylon-poly upper. It doesn’t hurt that its black-on-black design looks sharp, too. Read the full review. Weight: 17.6 oz (men’s) / 15.9 oz (women’s) “Old-school substance without the old-school break-in period” is how our reviewer described The North Face Offtrail Hike LT Mid GTX. An EVA midsole paired with a flexible rockguard provided cushion underfoot, while a well-padded upper and heel cup kept the foot comfortable. The result? A supportive hiking boot for weak ankles that our testers said felt like “a firm hug” even when the trail got rough. Read the full review. The Meindl Air Revolution Alpine 4.1 isn’t for everyone: With its stiff sole, heavy weight, and aggressive tread, this mountaineering-adjacent hiking boot is best for rough terrain, heavy loads, and long stretches above treeline. But we were shocked by the out-of-box comfort and extreme breathability, too. Read the full review. Weight: 20.8 oz (men’s) / 20.5 oz (women’s) Think of the Arc’teryx Konseal Trek as James Bond’s car: Its slick looks conceal “an arsenal of protection,” as our reviewer noted. Among its tricks: a bonded Gore-Tex membrane that provides waterproofing while keeping the boot slim; a mid-height, lightly-padded cuff outfitted with a Kevlar exterior for durability even on talus-strewn slopes; and a carbon fiber shank worked into the EVA midsole, so your ride is both comfortable and stable. Read the full review. First, look at the cuff: You want an upper that’s stiff enough to support your joint if you stumble or step on a loose rock, but not so stiff that you can’t maintain a natural stride on the tail. Which of those you prioritize depends on your objectives: Long days on relatively smooth trail call for softer support, while stiffer boots may help prevent injury on steep, loose ascents. Pay attention to the padding on the cuff, which should cradle your ankle rather than squeeze it. Midsole construction can also make a big difference in how a boot feels on the trail: An EVA midsole will feel bouncier and softer, more akin to a running shoe, while a PU midsole will provide a somewhat stiffer, more supportive ride, though often at a weight penalty. A shank, often made of a material like carbon fiber, will provide additional stiffness and structural support to the sole, though it should still allow your foot to flex naturally. Finally, pay attention to the outsole; while it may not play a role in supporting your ankle directly, a grippy tread can help prevent stumbles and slips, which can lead to injuries. Softer rubber will grip better on hard surfaces, though it will shorten the boot’s lifespan as it wears away faster. A harder, less pliable rubber may feel more slippery on surfaces like slickrock, but can grip well on soft trail, allowing its tread to “bite” into the path. Mostly we just let our testers do what they do best: walk. We called in dozens of different hiking boots and shoes and handed them out to 15 testers with instructions to put on some serious miles. They took short hikes and 30-mile backpacking trips, on-trail and off. They scrambled up peaks and down canyons, logging more than 700 miles in total. As they trekked along, we asked them to consider everything from fit to grip, cushioning to stability. Because pack weight can influence all these variables, we had them hike with both light loads and heavy packs. And to understand how boots and shoes performed in different weather conditions and environments, we spread testers and samples across the continent, from coastal British Columbia to New England’s windy summits. After at least two testers have tried every shoe, we have them fill out a detailed questionnaire. Then we send them back out with more shoes. The process is ongoing and endless. With every review we compare the results to all the other hikers we’ve tested over the years. Because ultimately we’re not just looking for the best new hiking boots for weak ankles, we want the best hiking boots for weak ankles, period. Category manager Wisconsin-based Blair Braverman is a long-distance dogsledder who loves hiking whenever she’s not mushing. Her longest backpacking trip was the 400-mile Oregon Coast Trail, and her favorite is Colorado’s Four-Pass Loop.

item.title: REVIEW: Brother MFC-J5110DW Review: A Tireless Inkjet Workhorse for Busy Small Offices
item.description:
Source: PCMag
At first glance, the Brother MFC-J5110DW INKvestment color inkjet all-in-one (AIO) printer looks essentially identical to the MFC-J5010DW, our Editors' Choice inkjet AIO for micro and busy home offices. However, it has additional paper capacity and a larger touch-screen control panel. It also adds support for PCL and BR-Script 3 (Brother's PostScript emulation) for offices that need either, and a faster first-page-out (FPO) time, which makes it much faster overall on our tests despite matching speed ratings on the two printers' spec sheets. These extras boost the list price to $359.99. They also move the printer into the overkill range for home offices, while making it a stellar choice for busy micro offices and an Editors' Choice-winning inkjet AIO for small offices and workgroups. One of the MFC-J5110DW's strongest points is its robust paper handling. For printing, it offers two 250-sheet paper drawers, plus a 100-sheet multipurpose tray, each of which can handle stacks of paper up to legal size and auto-duplex as well. The 600-sheet total capacity is easily enough to keep paper refills down to about once a week on average, even if you hit Brother's 2,500-page peak recommended monthly duty cycle every month. Keep in mind, however, that the recommendation is for printed pages. If you print mostly in duplex, that translates to 1,250 sheets of paper. For scanning, you'll find a letter-size flatbed plus a 50-sheet duplexing automatic document feeder (ADF) that can scan both sides of up to legal-size paper in a single pass. That's a tremendous time-saver versus either manual duplexing or reversing ADFs that scan one side, turn over the page, and then scan the second side separately. Single-pass duplexing also works for copying and faxing. Menu options on the 4.3-inch front panel touch screen let you copy both one-sided and two-sided originals to either one- or two-sided copies. And for both copying and faxing, you can specify whether duplex pages should be flipped on the short edge or the long edge. The printer can also scan to and print from a cloud or local email server, a USB key plugged into the USB Type-A port to the left of the touch screen, popular cloud sites (Google Drive, Evernote, OneDrive, OneNote, Dropbox, Box, and SharePoint Online), and an assortment of Brother's own cloud apps (Easy Scan to E-Mail, Scan to Mobile, Cloud Secure Print, and more). In addition, you can use menu commands to easily create customized shortcuts—giving you a second copy command defined for legal-size paper, for example, and a third one for duplexing with letter-size. Each is added to the menus, with a maximum of 64 shortcuts (including the 13 that ship with the machine) spread across eight menu screens, each with eight shortcuts. Larger offices and workgroups in a larger company may also want to take advantage of the printer's security features. Administrators can set up a secure function lock that prevents users from entering front-panel menu commands without first identifying themselves with a PIN or ID card. (To use a card, however, you have to add a third-party USB card reader.) Administrators can also define different PINs or cards to unlock different sets of features, including secure printing. One inevitable downside of highly capable paper handling is that it increases size and weight. The MFC-J5110DW weighs 37.8 pounds and measures 13.4 by 17.1 by 17.3 inches, which means you'll probably want some help moving it into place. However, the physical setup itself is standard. Load paper, then insert the cyan, yellow, magenta, and black ink cartridges. After the printer finishes the initial step of loading ink from the cartridges, the installation routine takes you through a nozzle check, prints an alignment page, waits for you to place the page on the scan bed, then scans it and aligns itself for you. If you don't have a preference or company requirement for a particular driver, you can go to Brother's website, download either the EasySetup or Full Software package to your system, and install it. However, in addition to the standard driver included in either of these downloads, Brother also offers a PCL driver and Brother's PostScript emulation (BR-Script 3). If your company standard is PCL or PostScript, or you use programs that require PostScript, you'll need to download the individual driver separately to install it. Both choices are in the Drivers section of the Downloads page. (Note that to see them, you need to choose the Show All link in that section.) For my tests, I used Ethernet to connect both the printer and our standard Windows testbed PC to a network, then downloaded and installed the package with the standard driver. If you prefer, you can connect by USB, Wi-Fi, or Wi-Fi Direct instead. Also note that the download options include Arm drivers for Windows 11, which the company says offer full support for printing and partial support for scanning. For mobile printing, the printer also supports AirPrint and Mopria, as well as both Android and iOS versions of Brother Mobile Connect. The app, which also supports scanning to mobile devices, lets you connect to the printer using either Wi-Fi Direct or by first connecting to the same network the printer is on. Brother used to say that its INKvestment printers were tank printers, because they pumped ink from the cartridges into tanks inside the printer. However, there are now two types of INKvestment printers. One kind, which Brother calls simply "INKvestment printers," still uses ink that comes in high-yield cartridges. The other kind, which Brother calls "INKvestment Tank printers," uses ink supplied in bottles that you pour into the tanks, as you do with tank printers from Canon, Epson, and HP. The general rule is that INKvestment printers that use cartridges have lower running costs than traditional cartridge printers, but higher costs than tank printers that ship ink in bottles. More important, the rule applies to the MFC-J5110DW. Ink cartridges for the printer come in three capacities and are available individually or in packs of two to four. The super-high-yield cartridges, which offer the lowest running cost, work out to 1.5 cents per mono page and 8.25 cents per standard color page, assuming you buy the black ink in the two-cartridge pack. As always, keep in mind that when comparing printer costs, it's the total cost of ownership that matters, not the running cost alone. (For details, take a look at How to Save Money on Your Next Printer.) To judge the Brother MFC-J5110DW's performance in context, I compared its test results with those of three other AIOs that include faxing: the MFC-J5010DW, the Brother MFC-L2900DW XL, and the Epson EcoTank ET-4950. The MFC-L2900DW XL mono laser printer is only slightly less expensive than the MFC-J5110DW, and it's one of our top picks for a micro to small office. The ET-4950 is an inkjet with a higher list price than the other models in the group but lower running costs. As the chart above shows, for simplex printing, the fastest in the group was the MFC-L2900DW XL, as you might expect given mono laser technology's reputation for speed. However, the MFC-J5110DW came in a fairly close second, largely due to its faster first-page-out (FPO) time. For pages 2 through 12 of our 12-page Word file, the Brother laser, at 35ppm, beat both Brother inkjets by 10ppm. For the full 12 pages, however, the laser came in at 26ppm compared with 23ppm for the MFC-J5110DW, a difference of only 4 seconds, thanks to the inkjet's 11-second head start from a faster first page. In real-world use, that short FPO time will make the MFC-J5110DW faster for text documents of only a few pages. However, the MFC-L2900DW XL will have a significant advantage overall if you print many documents that are tens of pages long or longer. The MFC-J5010DW matched the second-place MFC-J5110DW when not including the first page. However, its longer FPO time dropped it to third place for both the Word file and the full business applications suite (latter shown below). The ET-4950 was definitively the slowest overall. The printers also finished the full business applications suite, which adds color and graphics, in the same order as for the Word file. What our charts don't show is that the MFC-J5110DW color printer was 9 seconds faster than the laser mono printer overall when printing the test's PDF, Excel, and PowerPoint files, largely thanks to its shorter FPO time. For duplex printing for the full 12-page Word file, the MFC-J5110DW came in first overall, as well as for the first sheet out (pages 1 and 2) and for pages 3 through 12. So if you print mostly in duplex, it will be the fastest in the group. For photo printing, the MFC-J5110DW's average speed for printing our 4-by-6-inch photos was a relatively slow 56 seconds, largely because, unlike most inkjets, it switches to Best quality mode when set for the recommended paper we used. Text quality in our tests was close to top tier for an inkjet, making it good enough for most purposes. All of the non-italic fonts we test that you'd most likely use in business documents were easily readable at 4 points, while the one italic font cleared that bar at 5 points. Of the two heavily stylized fonts we include with thick strokes, one was easily readable at 8 points, while the other, which is harder to render well, was easily readable at 10 points. The default graphics settings delivered nicely saturated, eye-catching color on plain paper. I saw some minor banding, but only in two full-page graphics. Most fills and gradients were appropriately smooth. The printer also did an impressive job with thin lines, including a single-pixel-wide line on a black background that many printers turn into a dashed line or fail to print entirely. For photos, using Brother's BP71GLTR photo paper, the printer delivered acceptably accurate, saturated color, neutral grays for black-and-white prints, and good contrast and shadow detail, scoring at the high end of drugstore quality overall. In our water-resistance tests on plain paper, black ink smudged slightly when I gently wiped off water drops. Color inks didn't smudge, but they lost saturation when transferred to what I was wiping with. Text on plain paper stood up to a single stroke of a highlighter but smudged slightly if I went over the same text a second time. On photo paper, both color and black inks resisted smudging. - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. Of the four printers mentioned here, the Brother MFC-J5110DW is our favorite for a small office by enough to make it our new top pick for a small-office inkjet. However, each of the others profiled here offers something that might make it the better fit for your needs. The MFC-L2900DW XL has the fastest simplex speed for long documents, making it a tempting choice if you don't print much in duplex, don't need color, and regularly print long documents that take advantage of its speed. And as the only laser printer, it has the most water-resistant output in the group. The ET-4950, in contrast, is the slowest in the group and the most expensive, but it's also the only true tank-based printer. Its ink, supplied in bottles, offers low enough running costs that, if you print enough pages, it can easily give you a lower total cost of ownership over its lifetime than any of the other three models. As I mentioned above, the MFC-J5010DW is our Editors' Choice winner for AIO inkjet printers for micro offices. It offers almost all the same features as the MFC-J5110DW, but has a lower paper capacity and a slower FPO time in our tests, making it best reserved for somewhat lighter use. On the other hand, it's also the smaller and lighter of the two, and it costs less. The differences make it a better fit than its big brother for a smaller office—namely, a micro or home office. In contrast, the MFC-J5110DW combines three paper feeds, more than double the paper capacity of any of the others, and high speed—particularly for short documents and duplex printing. That's more than enough to earn it our Editors' Choice award for a small-office color inkjet. item.title: REVIEW: Review: Apple's M6 iMac is pricey, but it's still a good choice for a clean desk

So I wanted to write about this new iMac from the perspective of that entry-level iMac buyer, who chooses the iMac because it’s simple and then uses it until it breaks. What does a new iMac get you if you’re stepping up from the M1 model or comparing it against an older refurbished M4 model? Without any real external updates, what makes this iMac iteration interesting? If you haven’t used an Apple Silicon-era iMac before, here’s a brief primer. The new iMac is much thinner than the older aluminum Intel models. Its front is mostly one big 24-inch screen, surrounded on all sides by a relatively thick white bezel (I still wish black were at least an option, but Apple apparently doesn’t agree). White bezel aside, it’s by far Apple’s most colorful computer. The iMacs ship with color-matched fronts, backs, stands, keyboards, mice, trackpads, and cables. item.title: SALES: Great Hydration is About More than Just Electrolytes

Hydration is not only an essential component of pre-, mid- and post-workout performance. It’s an essential part of everyday life. Electrolytes are a particular point of focus among performance athletes. Electrolytes are the minerals that help maintain the balance of fluids inside and outside your body’s cells. This is a critical consideration when it comes to high-exertion workouts where you’re losing lots of fluids through sweat. The market is more saturated (pun intended) than ever with tablets, powders and pouches galore to help you optimize and maximize your electrolyte intake. But hydration doesn’t have to be as complicated as all that—and the conversation surrounding electrolytes doesn’t have to be reserved for elite athletes. It can be an everyday consideration for your morning walk, a quick out-and-back hike, or your daily commute to the office. And it all starts with a single coconut. That’s the mission behind Harmless Harvest, a California-based company championing the coconut, turning a remarkable fruit into a remarkable lineup of products. It’s new pantry-friendly coconut water contains one ingredient: 100% coconut water with no added sugar or preservatives. The simplicity of their products ladder up to the simplicity of the brand’s philosophy—that great taste, quality ingredients, and premium tasting hydration should be for everyone to enjoy. Uncomplicated hydration doesn’t have to be a statistic for you to overanalyze—it can be an intentional and enjoyable part of your everyday life. So what’s so great about a simple bottle of coconut water? Well, it’s just that: the simplicity. All on its own, coconut water delivers naturally occurring electrolytes, including potassium, to support everyday hydration. Unlike the formulated hydration drinks, tablets and powders that rely on added electrolytes, coconut water provides those muscle-supporting, fluid-balancing minerals into every bottle of Harmless Harvest coconut water naturally. Every bottle is made with a single ingredient with that naturally sweet coconut taste that’s completely delicious and refreshing. From your pantry to wherever the day takes you, Harmless Harvest’s newest coconut water makes it easier than ever to keep great-tasting hydration close at hand. With no refrigeration required, you can keep bottles at room temperature until you’re ready to enjoy. Grab a bottle on the way to yoga, before a big day on the slopes, or just on the way to work. And unlike the traditional flash pasteurization commonly used by beverage producers, Harmless Harvest’s optimized heat treatment and micro-filtration preserves the fruit’s natural sweetness and nutrients, so you’re getting everything the mighty coconut has to offer. Another question you might be asking is why is Harmless Harvest’s coconut water pink? Rather than using additives to control color variation from bottle to bottle, the company has embraced the pink hue that can come with the interaction between the coconut water’s antioxidants and natural elements like light and temperature. Harmless Harvest’s commitment to sustainability and environmentally conscious practices extends beyond the bottle, too. The brand works with coconut growers in Thailand to source ethically farmed, non-GMO coconuts and also invests in initiatives that support farmers and their communities. These conscientious business practices aim to bring you products that you can sip with peace of mind. Coconut water may not be the first thing you think to grab before a big workout or after a long run. It’s not a product that we typically associate with performance and recovery, but perhaps that’s the whole point. Don’t get us wrong, electrolytes are important, but in the age of optimization, where every mile, calorie and ounce of water is tracked, logged, and analyzed, it’s good to get back to the basics. Being well-hydrated shouldn’t be reserved for when you’re pushing your body to its limits. Harmless Harvest’s mission is to show that just like general wellness, proper hydration goes beyond a numerical value—it’s about being mindful and listening to your body, one sip at a time. Harmless Harvest creates delicious, premium coconut-based beverages and foods, crafted with care for people and the planet. Known for its naturally hydrating coconut water, the brand is committed to exceptional taste, responsibly sourced ingredients, and sustainable farming practices. Its mission is simple: make remarkable products while doing less harm and more good.

item.title: SALES: Pre-orders for some Apple Home Collection devices will open November 13
item.description:
Source: Engadget
Pre-orders for some Apple Home Collection devices will open November 13 You can lock in orders for two LG cameras and a video doorbell. On the same day that the Apple HomeView smart display and refreshed Apple TV 4K hit stores, pre-orders will open for some accessories in the Apple Home Collection. Apple confirmed to Engadget that you'll be able to pre-order the LG indoor camera, outdoor camera and video doorbell on November 13. Those three devices, which Apple and LG collaborated on, will be the first Apple Home Collection accessories to ship. They're slated to arrive in December. Apple hasn't revealed exactly when other products in the lineup — including thermostats and door locks — will be available, but the company has said some will be available next month with the rest debuting in early 2027. The indoor camera can capture 2.5K footage of what's going on in your home while you're away, giving you a way to keep an eye on your pets, for instance. It has low-light color night vision and infrared (IR) night vision support. The camera, which costs $200 and can detect people and pets, can tilt up when you're out and down when you're home — this can be managed automatically through the Home app or manually by pressing a button. The outdoor camera can recognize faces, pets and deliveries. It too supports low-light color night vision, IR night vision and 2.5K video capture. The camera has IP65-rated protection from rain and dust and a two‑way talk function. As with the indoor camera, you'll get 10 days' worth of event video history via iCloud+. There's built-in storage too. The standard outdoor camera costs $300 and a version with a floodlight will run you $400. As for the $250 video doorbell, that has a dual-camera design that can pick up (for instance) visitors and packages simultaneously — a 2.5K camera faces forward and a Full HD one points downward. You'll be able to view either feed separately in the Home app and chat to whoever's at your door using the two-way talk function. When someone rings the doorbell, HomeView and HomePod devices will sound a chime. You'll get notifications on other Apple devices too. Again, there's low-light color night vision and IR night vision support, along with event video history in iCloud+ and built-in storage. item.title: SALES: Best AI Reputation Management Firms in 2026: Top Picks for AI Visibility & LLM Reputation (vs. Traditional ORM)
item.description:
Source: Digital Trends
When someone asks ChatGPT, Gemini or Perplexity about your business, the answer they get is now your first impression. ChatGPT alone reached 900 million weekly active users in February 2026. Traditional online reputation management was built to push bad links off page one. AI visibility and LLM reputation management is about what the answer itself says. That shift has created a new category, and only a handful of companies work in it. Some are service firms that change what AI says. Others are software platforms that measure it. Below, we rank the best AI reputation management firms and platforms for 2026, explain how this work differs from traditional ORM, and show which option fits which need. What is AI visibility and LLM reputation management? AI visibility and LLM reputation management is the work of monitoring and shaping what large language models like ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity and Google AI Overviews say about a person or brand. It covers two jobs: making sure accurate, positive information shows up in AI answers, and removing or correcting the false, outdated or harmful sources those answers are built on. How is it different from traditional ORM? Traditional online reputation management and AI reputation management share the same goal, but they work on different surfaces. ○ Traditional ORM: Ten blue links on Google, plus review sites. ○ AI reputation management: A single generated answer that blends many sources into one story. ○ Traditional ORM: A negative link is one result among many, and few people scroll past page one. ○ AI reputation management: A negative claim can become the whole answer. When Google shows an AI summary, users click a source inside it on just 1% of visits, according to Pew Research Center. ○ Traditional ORM: Suppression, publishing positive pages that outrank the bad one. ○ AI reputation management: Removing or correcting the source, because AI tools can still find and cite a page that’s been pushed to page three. ○ Traditional ORM: Keyword rankings. ○ AI reputation management: What each AI platform says, which sources it cites and how often your brand is recommended. We looked at four things: whether each company tracks what AI platforms say, whether it can change those answers, how many AI platforms it covers, and who it’s built for. Direct removal capability carried the most weight, since monitoring alone tells you about a problem without solving it. Several entries below are software platforms rather than service firms. We included them because many businesses will use a platform alongside a service firm, and knowing the difference helps you pick the right mix. The best AI reputation management firms and platforms in 2026 What they do: Reputation Resolutions is a full-service online reputation management firm based in Englewood, Colorado, and our pick for the top spot among the best AI reputation management firms. It is the only firm on this list that combines AI monitoring with hands-on removal of the content behind harmful answers. Its team audits what every major AI platform says about a client, traces each claim to the page it came from, removes or corrects that source, and builds accurate content to take its place. Standout capability: Removal at the source. Most companies on this list measure AI visibility. Reputation Resolutions changes it, with platform-specific work for ChatGPT, Gemini and Google AI Overviews. It has also built free tools that put that removal expertise in anyone’s hands: RemoveNews.ai writes a personalized removal request for a news article and finds the editor’s direct contact in about 60 seconds, and a free court record removal scan finds court and arrest records copied onto people-search and mugshot sites. Track record: More than a decade of removal work, more than 5,000 clients in over 40 countries, and recognition from Forbes and Inc. Magazine. Best for: Individuals, executives and businesses dealing with false, outdated or damaging AI answers, and anyone who needs the problem fixed rather than just reported. “We start every AI engagement the same way,” Will says. “We ask each platform what your customers would ask, record every source it cites, and then go after those sources one by one. That’s the only fix that holds across every AI tool at once.” What they do: Minc Law is a Cleveland-based law firm focused on internet defamation, online harassment and content removal. The firm says it has removed more than 200,000 pieces of defamatory and damaging online content and litigated more than 350 cases in 26 states and five countries. Standout capability: Legal action. When false content won’t come down through outreach or platform policies, Minc Law can send demand letters, pursue defamation claims and work to unmask anonymous posters. Best for: Cases where the source behind a harmful AI answer is defamatory and needs a legal remedy. It pairs well with a removal-focused reputation firm: legal pressure on one side, removal and AI reputation work on the other. What they do: Birdeye is a review and customer experience platform for multi-location brands. Its Birdeye AI Search product tracks brand and location-level visibility across ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, Google AI Overviews, Google AI Mode, Claude and Grok. Standout capability: Location-level AI visibility scoring, citation tracking and sentiment analysis, tied to its review management tools. Best for: Franchises and multi-location brands that want to monitor AI visibility location by location and keep review volume up. Keep in mind: Birdeye is software. It can show you a negative source and help you publish better content, but it doesn’t remove third-party articles, records or posts. What they do: Yext manages business listings and brand data across search engines, maps and directories. In March 2025 it launched Yext Scout, an AI search and competitive intelligence agent that tracks how brands appear across ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, Grok and Google. Standout capability: Keeping business facts accurate and consistent everywhere AI tools look, with competitor benchmarking built in. Best for: Enterprise and multi-location brands whose main AI problem is inconsistent or outdated business information. Keep in mind: Yext focuses on data you control, like listings and web content. It isn’t built to remove negative content published by others. What they do: Podium is a customer communication platform for local businesses that combines messaging, review requests and payments. Its AI Employee handles lead response and appointment booking around the clock. Standout capability: Generating a steady flow of fresh, positive reviews, which feed the review sites AI tools pull from when they describe local businesses. Best for: Local service businesses such as auto dealers, home services, dental and medical practices that want more reviews and faster customer response. Keep in mind: Podium builds positive signals. It doesn’t track AI answers directly or remove harmful content. What they do: Vendasta is a white-label software platform for agencies and resellers that serve small businesses. Its Reputation AI product monitors reviews across more than 100 sites and uses an AI agent to post personalized review replies. Standout capability: White-label delivery, so agencies can offer review and reputation tools under their own brand. Best for: Marketing agencies that want to add reputation services for many small business clients at once. Keep in mind: Vendasta is a toolset for agencies, not a removal service, and its focus is reviews rather than AI answers. What they do: Profound is an answer engine optimization (AEO) analytics platform that shows brands how often AI models mention them and in what context, across ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini and Google AI Overviews. The company raised $180 million at a $1.8 billion valuation in September 2026. Standout capability: Large-scale measurement of AI share of voice and citation patterns for enterprise marketing teams. Best for: Enterprise marketing and SEO teams that want detailed data on how their brand performs in AI answers compared with competitors. Keep in mind: Profound measures and optimizes visibility. It doesn’t handle reputation crises or remove harmful content. Which option is right for you? ● If AI is saying something false or damaging about you: Start with Reputation Resolutions. It’s the only option here that traces AI claims to their sources and removes them. ● If the source is defamatory and needs legal action: Add Minc Law. ● If you run many locations and want ongoing AI and review monitoring: Look at Birdeye or Yext. ● If you’re a local business that needs more reviews: Podium fits. ● If you’re an agency serving small businesses: Vendasta fits. ● If you’re an enterprise team measuring AI share of voice: Profound fits. AI visibility and LLM reputation management is quickly replacing page-one rankings as the measure of how people see you. Monitoring platforms can tell you what AI says, and review tools can build positive signals, but changing a harmful answer means removing what it’s built on. For anyone comparing the best companies for AI reputation management, that’s the deciding question: can they change the answer, or only report it? On that test, Reputation Resolutions ranks first.

Look to Sony's 1979-inspired MDR-3R wired headphones, which also come in a special Stranger Things variant. For album lovers rediscovering the joy of the physical, "you'll always own this" music product (take that, Spotify!), I have several recommendations. There's the excellent Sony PS-LX5BT turntable, the Gadhouse MIKO cassette player or the kn5 CP1 portable CD player, all of which will make superb gifts. Oh, and if you want to go big (maybe they've had a tough year; maybe this is a Big Present), the Marshall Bromley 150 is a stunning Bluetooth speaker with loads of rock 'n' roll appeal, while the Creative XF1 are very capable desktop speakers. Whatever you buy them, you're getting a TechRadar approved audio product — don't forget the 'view details' tab for our product-specific coverage to help you further. And above all, enjoy some tunes while gift-wrapping! I've reviewed over 180 audio products since becoming a tech journalist, ranging from super-budget earbuds to high-end Hi-Res Audio music players. item.title: SALES: 15 Best Grand Canyon Hotels, Rentals, and Glampsites for Sleeping in Style Under the Stars
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
A mile deep and 277 miles long, the Grand Canyon is a jaw-droppingly majestic chasm in Arizona’s rust-red desert that’s speckled with pinyon pines. Standing on its edge, one can’t help but feel small, watching the mighty Colorado River churn vigorously along the ravine’s bottom. Whether you’re hoping for a challenging all-day hike to the canyon’s floor, a soul-stirring overlook near the visitor center, or a multi-day rafting expedition, this national park has all that (and more) in spades. It’s hardly a surprise that it drew more than 4.4 million visitors in 2025 alone, so you know you'll have some competition when it comes to finding the best place to stay nearby. Personally, I like to stay as close as possible to the park, to make the most of dreamy desert sunrises and maximize my time on the trails. Grand Canyon is famous for its historic lodges and quirky Route 66 nostalgia, which can make picking the perfect spot for your crew a little overwhelming. Cozy cabin or fancy, family-sized rental? Canvas glamping tent under the stars or a fun getaway that’s in the heart of the action? I’ve sorted through the hundreds of options so you don’t have to. Here are my favorite Grand Canyon hotels, glamping sites, vacation rentals, and cabins for a memorable stay in and around this utterly striking national park. How to plan a trip to Grand Canyon National Park When is the best time to visit Grand Canyon National Park? With an elevation spanning 2,000 feet to 8,000 feet, Grand Canyon experiences a wide range of temperatures on any given day. Thus, the best season to visit greatly depends on what your adventure priorities are. If you’re planning to raft “the big ditch” with a guide, go between April and October for warm, sunny days that perfectly contrast the 50-degree Colorado River. Hoping to hike to the bottom and camp at Bright Angel? Don your favorite traction devices atop the canyon to crunch through seasonal ice and book a backcountry permit for late fall, winter, or early spring. Auto tourists who want to explore the canyon’s south rim by car can travel in virtually any season—just be prepared for crowds in summer months and occasional snow closures at the height of winter. Lastly, a good rule of thumb for intrepid travelers hiking down into the canyon is that you’ll gain roughly 5 degrees for every 1,000 feet you descend. Plan on it being 20 degrees warmer at the bottom of the canyon than it is at the rim. The National Park Service (NPS) does not recommend hiking to the bottom of the canyon during summer months, as temperatures at Phantom Ranch often surpass 100 degrees. How do you get to Grand Canyon National Park? If you’re planning to fly in, the closest major airports are Sky Harbor International in Phoenix and Harry Reid International in Las Vegas, but both are at least a three-hour drive away, so you’ll want to rent a car and crank up the tunes to brave the journey. Regional airports are scattered around the area, most notably in small-but-commercial Flagstaff, Sedona, and Tusayan. There’s also a vintage train service that runs daily from Williams, Arizona. Notably, Grand Canyon National Park is a stone’s throw away from one of the most iconic road trips the US has to offer–historic Route 66. Running from Chicago all the way to the Pacific Coast in Santa Monica, California, this legendary trip ventures across northern Arizona on Interstate 40. What are the best things to do in Grand Canyon National Park? Spanning 23 breathtaking miles between Grand Canyon Village and the Desert View area, Desert View Drive is the only scenic byway in the park that’s open year-round to private vehicles. Enjoy Mary Colter’s iconic Desert View Watchtower, which was inspired by ancestral Puebloan architecture and features murals by Hopi artist Fred Kabotie, at the park’s far eastern edge. Another popular drive along the South Rim is the winding Hermit Road, which ends at the historic stone structure of Hermit’s Rest that date back to 1914. The drive is only open to private vehicles in December, January, and February; in all other months, travelers must use the park’s free shuttle system, hopping on and off at popular sites. Though the hiking distance between the canyon’s north and south rims is a scant 21 miles, the drive to get between the two is a circuitous 220 miles. As a result, only 10% of the national park’s visitors set foot on the just-as-striking North Rim. This high-elevation outpost (over 8,000 feet) and log cabin-style lodge have a shorter visitation season than the South Rim (you’ll have to travel there between May 15 and October 15 most years), but adventurous drivers desperate to escape the crowds should make a beeline for the pinyon and ponderosa pine–studded views of crumbling crimson sandstone along Cape Royal Road. Plus, you’ll be within easy driving distance of Zion, if you’d like to extend your journey. If you’re into hiking past dramatic vermillion outcroppings, secret waterfalls, and hanging gardens, you’re in the right place. The Grand Canyon also boasts some of the most stunning wheelchair-accessible paths in the country (check out the 13-mile, mostly-paved Rim Trail), as well as hamstring-busting overnight treks into the belly of the ravine. For an epic out-and-back excursion with much of the expansive red rock scenery you’d find on a longer jaunt, head to South Kaibab Trailhead and venture just under a mile downhill to the aptly named Ooh Aah Point. Want a little more bang for your buck? Continue down to Skeleton Point for a sweeping panorama of the Colorado River (six miles round trip). Bright Angel Trailhead is another iconic starting point for a day hike or overnight trek into the canyon. Lace up your boots for a three-mile round-trip stroll to the shade structure at Mile-and-a-Half Resthouse or, if you’re an experienced hiker looking to sweat, start early for an all-day 12-mile journey to jaw-dropping views of Plateau Point. Trekking to the bottom of the Grand Canyon and back is the stuff hiking bucket lists are made of. But due to midday heat and the extremely strenuous nature of these hikes, the National Park Service does not recommend aiming to complete such a journey in a single day. It’s highly recommended to nab a backcountry permit and camp overnight at one of the many below-the-rim sites (like Bright Angel Campground or Havasupai Gardens). Pro tip: Use the free park shuttle and create a loop starting at South Kaibab and ending at the Bright Angel Trailhead. Heading for the quieter North Rim? Tramp down the North Kaibab Trail for two miles (one-way) to Supai Tunnel. It’s rare that a national park offers a designated bike path along its most iconic sights, but at the Grand Canyon, visitors can spin for roughly 13 miles along the park’s dreamy South Rim vistas. BYO-bike or rent one at Canyon Adventures in the village, then steer onto the paved Greenway Trail to South Kaibab. Or, utilize the free shuttle system (yes, they’ve got bike racks) and ride the bus to Monument Creek Vista, then cruise along the South Rim to Hermits Rest. North Rim visitors hoping to escape that South Rim fervor can enjoy loads of rugged mountain biking. A 12-mile swath of the enormous, 800-mile Arizona Trail runs right through the park. Are there guided tours at Grand Canyon National Park? There are dozens of phenomenal guided tours available for guests who aren’t comfortable backpacking alone or want a unique type of experience. Mule rides are a storied part of the canyon’s past and how many early tourists ventured into the canyon (sometimes in full Victorian regalia). Though it might seem like a rough place for a working animal, mules are much better equipped to handle heat and steep, rocky terrain than their horse counterparts. Plus, these rides offer below-the-rim access for visitors with mobility concerns. Today, both short day trips and extended overnight ventures to Phantom Ranch on muleback are available for those looking to pay homage to a bygone era. For a brag-worthy addition to your hiking checklist, seek out Wildland Trekking’s guided rim-to-rim backpacking journeys (or, in winter, go big and test your skills on a rim-to-rim-to-rim hike). Craving something off the beaten path? The remote, five-day Hermit Loop offers miles of fire-red sandstone plateaus. I’d be remiss if I didn’t mention the second-to-none river rafting to be had at Grand Canyon National Park. Grand Canyon Expeditions and Western River Expeditions have been guiding for decades and both offer first-class service for intrepid travelers looking to go the distance on the mighty Colorado. item.title: SALES: Best monitors 2026: Top picks for gaming, 4K, HDR, and more
item.description:
Source: PCWorld
Need a new monitor for your PC? I’ve combed through scores of options to find the best monitors on the market right now. These picks are the result of hundreds of hours spent testing the latest models from Acer, Asus, BenQ, Dell, LG, Samsung, and other major brands. While my favorite monitor overall is an awesome choice for most people, I also have alternative options for budget shoppers, gamers, and those seeking the best HDR performance. After all, not everyone needs the same features from a monitor. You can find out more about how I evaluate monitors and what specs matter most below my list of recommendations. Why you should trust PCWorld for monitor reviews and buying advice: It’s in our name! PCWorld prides itself on PC hardware experience and expertise. We’ve been covering PCs since 1983, and we now review dozens of monitors every year. All of our recommendations have been personally tested and vetted by our expert reviewers, who’ve applied not only performance benchmarks but rigorous usability standards. Dell Ultrasharp U2724DE – Best monitor overall - Class-leading Thunderbolt and USB connectivity Who should buy the Dell Ultrasharp U2724DE? Dell’s Ultrasharp U2724DE is an incredibly versatile monitor that will satisfy most users. It’s great for home office productivity, good for gaming, and can handle more serious content creation workflows, like photo and video editing. The U2724DE has an IPS Black panel that roughly doubles the monitor’s contrast ratio (compared to other IPS monitors). It can’t beat a more expensive OLED or Mini-LED panel, but it’s still alluring. It also lacks the burn-in worries of OLED which, although unlikely to occur in mixed use, might become an issue if you spend all day working in Excel and plan to keep your monitor for as long as possible. Dell pairs the IPS Black panel with an enhanced 120Hz refresh rate. Upping the refresh rate greatly improves motion clarity and makes the U2724DE a viable display for gamers. That’s a big deal. It means you can buy one monitor for both work and play. The U2724DE goes all-in on connectivity. Thunderbolt 4, USB-C, USB-A, DisplayPort-in and -out, and HDMI are present. It even has a 2.5G Ethernet port. These features are ideal if you plan to connect a laptop over USB-C, as the U2724DE will greatly expand the laptop’s connectivity. Dell Ultrasharp U2724DE: Further considerations Resolution is the only notable downside. The U2724DE is a 1440p monitor, while many competitors in its price bracket offer 4K. This is often the trade-off made to hit monitor’s 120Hz refresh rate. For 4K goodness see the Dell U3225QE below. Just know that it’s almost 50 percent more expensive. - Solid build with ergonomic stand, tripod mount Who should buy the Acer Vero B247Y G? Value shoppers who want a good-quality, versatile monitor at a budget price will be pleased with the Acer Vero B247Y G. This 24-inch 1080p IPS monitor stands out with its surprising 120Hz refresh rate and Adaptive Sync support, making it suitable for both productivity and PC gaming. It also provides great image quality for a budget display, with above-average scores in contrast ratio and brightness, as well as good color performance. Build quality exceeds expectations, too, with a fully ergonomic stand that offers height, tilt, swivel, and even pivot adjustments—a rarity in budget displays. The monitor’s clear on-screen menu system provides easy access to various image settings, while the inclusion of both modern (HDMI, DisplayPort) and legacy (VGA) connections ensures compatibility with a wide range of devices. Acer Vero B247Y G: Further considerations Though it’s possible to find a less expensive 24-inch 1080p monitor, the Vero B247Y G justifies its slightly higher price through quality-of-life improvements, and it still manages to limbo under $150 when discounted (which it often is). It’s hard to find a more well-rounded budget monitor. Pixio PX248 Wave – Best budget gaming monitor - Attractive design, especially in unique colorways - Built-in speakers are surprisingly decent - Solid color accuracy and respectable gamut Who should buy the Pixio PX248 Wave? This is a great budget monitor for gamers who want more than a no-frills display. The Pixio PX248 Wave distinguishes itself from other budget options with a colorful, stylish design, and solid motion performance, for an enticing price of $159.99. Pixio offers this monitor in four colorways: black, white, blue, and pink. The latter two are rather special, as only a handful of monitors — like the more expensive Samsung M8 Smart Monitor — offer similarly out-of-the-box colors. The stand matches the monitor’s colorway, and Pixio even offers an optional color-coordinated monitor arm for those who want to go all-in on a particular desktop vibe. The monitor’s 24-inch Fast IPS display boasts a 200Hz refresh rate that delivers fluid motion. Image quality is reasonable, too, as the PX248 Wave delivers respectable color accuracy and coverage, making it suitable for both gaming and casual content creation. It has built-in speakers, too. Pixio PX248 Wave: Further considerations Despite its visual appeal, the PX248 Wave sticks to the basics with connectivity, which includes HDMI 2.0 and DisplayPort 1.4. USB connectivity isn’t available. The included stand is also basic, as it only adjusts for tilt, and the menu controls could be more user-friendly. Most competitors at this price point have a similar display panel wrapped in a more generic black, gray, or charcoal case. Pixio’s PX248 Wave manages to match them in image quality and beat them on looks, yet it stays on a budget. - Gamma, color temperature slightly off-target Who should buy the MSI MPG 272URX QD-OLED? For anyone who wants a high-performance gaming monitor, the MSI MPG 272URX QD-OLED should be at the top of your list. This 26.5-inch display delivers stunning 4K resolution with an ultra-smooth 240Hz refresh rate in a cutting-edge OLED panel. It’s an excellent choice for gamers who want both visual clarity and fluid motion. With its 240Hz refresh rate, the MSI delivers fast-paced gaming yet maintains the deep contrast and vibrant colors that OLED monitors are known for. It also supports Adaptive Sync for smooth frame pacing. MSI MPG 272URX QD-OLED: Further considerations The QD-OLED panel offers excellent contrast and color accuracy, which makes it a solid pick for creative professionals and anyone who enjoys watching HDR movies. Connectivity is also generous, with HDMI 2.1, DisplayPort 2.1a, and USB-C inputs, as well as 98 watts of USB Power Delivery for charging laptops or tablets. The design is a bit plain, but the stand is sturdy and fully adjustable, which is far more important. The MSI MPG 272URX is more expensive than 1440p OLED alternatives, which can be found for under $800. But if 4K clarity and a fluid 240Hz refresh rate are what you’re after, this monitor is worth the investment. - Useful design with small stand and ergonomic adjustment - Includes USB-C with up to 98 watts of Power Delivery - Wide range of image quality adjustments - 3440×1440 resolution is adequate, but not sharp - HDR brightness is only competitive in some situations Who should buy the MSI MPG 341CQR QD-OLED X36? The MSI MPG 341CQR QD-OLED X36 is the ultrawide monitor for shoppers who don’t want to sacrifice image quality or versatility. Its 5th-generation Samsung tandem QD-OLED panel delivers effectively infinite contrast, a wide color gamut spanning 100 percent sRGB and 98 percent DCI-P3, and excellent color accuracy, making it a serious contender for creative work as well as gaming. Its 360Hz refresh rate delivers great motion clarity, and the monitor’s VESA DisplayHDR True Black 500 certification provides solid real-world HDR performance. Connectivity is a strength. A USB-C port with 98 watts of Power Delivery means you can drive the display and charge a MacBook or thin-and-light Windows laptop through a single cable—a feature that’s still not guaranteed on gaming monitors. The price also works in the monitor’s favor. At $899.99, the MPG 341CQR sits just under the $1,000 mark, which makes it a good value given its excellent image quality and extensive feature set. MSI MPG 341CQR QD-OLED X36: Further considerations Pixel density is the major trade-off you accept with any 34-inch 1440p ultrawide. At roughly 110 pixels per inch, the MPG 341CQR is noticeably softer than a 27-inch 4K panel. It’s not a dealbreaker for most uses, but if sharpness matters you’ll need to stick to a widescreen panel. The monitor also ships without speakers, so budget for external audio. Dell Ultrasharp U3225QE – Best 4K monitor - Thunderbolt 4, USB-C, Ethernet, and 140 watts of Power Delivery - New generation of IPS Black boosts contrast ratio - Excellent sharpness from 31.5-inch 4K panel - Contrast ratio is good for an IPS panel - HDR brightness is decent, but contrast remains limited Who should buy the Dell U3225QE? This is a great choice for professionals who want a top-of-the-line home office monitor. The U3225QE has it all: a sharp 31.5-inch 4K IPS Black panel with excellent color accuracy and an above-average contrast ratio for a productivity monitor. The 120Hz refresh rate enhances responsiveness, making tasks like scrolling through documents and multitasking smoother. The ergonomic stand provides height, tilt, swivel, and portrait mode adjustments, and the anti-glare coating ensures comfortable viewing in various lighting conditions. In addition to all that, the U3225QE’s mitigates the need for external docks and adapters, with generous connectivity. It features Thunderbolt 4 / USB-C ports with 140W of Power Delivery—enough to charge most laptops—along with HDMI, DisplayPort, and a secondary DisplayPort for daisy-chaining multiple monitors. A built-in 2.5Gbps Ethernet port ensures a fast and stable wired network connection, a rare feature among monitors. It also offers six USB-A ports, a pop-out USB hub with quick-access USB-C and USB-A ports, and KVM switch functionality for seamless switching between two connected PCs. While it lacks built-in speakers and its HDR performance is limited, the U3225QE’s extensive connectivity and high-quality display make it a standout choice for professionals who need a central hub for their workspace. Want a smaller version of this monitor? Check out the Dell Ultrasharp U2725QE. It has a similar 4K IPS Black display panel and Thunderbolt 4 / USB-C connectivity. Asus ProArt Display 5K PA27JCV – Best 5K monitor - Includes USB-C with 96 watts Power Delivery - Lots of menu options and customization Who should buy the ProArt Display 5K PA27JCV? The ProArt Display 5K PA27JCV is perfect for content creators, programmers, designers, and anyone who values ultra-sharp image quality and accurate colors for productivity work. With a true 5K resolution (5120×2880) on a 27-inch panel, the ProArt Display 5K packs an incredibly crisp 218 pixels per inch. That’s much sharper than 5K ultrawides and nearly matches Apple’s Pro Display XDR. Text is crisp and hi-res photos look lifelike. The ProArt Display 5K’s color performance and brightness solidify its position. The monitor covers 100 percent of both sRGB and DCI-P3 color spaces, plus 91 percent of AdobeRGB, making it ideal for content creation. Its impressive 578-nit brightness ensures excellent visibility in any lighting condition, too. ProArt Display 5K PA27JCV: Further considerations Most compelling is the PA27JCV’s unmatched value proposition. At $800, it’s the most affordable true 5K monitor available as of early 2025. While it has some limitations, like a 60Hz refresh rate and modest contrast ratio, these are minor tradeoffs. It delivers super-sharp 5K resolution, professional-grade color performance, and outstanding value. - Tack-sharp 6K resolution at a new low price - Attractive design and highly functional stand - Thunderbolt 4 with some downstream USB connectivity - Great brightness and good color performance - HDR is supported but doesn’t look its best - Only 60Hz with limited Adaptive Sync support Who should buy the Asus ProArt Display 6K PA32QCV? If you want a 32-inch 6K monitor that delivers exceptional sharpness and strong color performance without the sky-high prices usually attached to this resolution, the ProArt PA32QCV is an easy recommendation. It’s ideal for professionals, prosumers, and creatives—especially Mac users—who need precise visuals, solid brightness, and Thunderbolt 4 connectivity with 96 watts of power delivery. While it doesn’t claim the very top spot in every technical category, particularly in contrast and HDR performance, its combination of resolution, usability, and value is unmatched. The ProArt also benefits from attractive design, a highly functional ergonomic stand, and a wide range of options that provide precise monitor adjustment. These features make it easy to tune and calibrate the monitor to fit your needs. Asus ProArt Display 6K PA32QCV: Further considerations Shoppers who want additional features should know there are other 6K monitors that provide more connectivity or higher-end capabilities. Dell’s UltraSharp U3224KB, for example, offers an IPS Black panel, integrated 4K webcam, Ethernet, and more powerful Thunderbolt 4 power delivery, making it a great fit for heavy collaboration workflows. MacBook users may also want to look at Apple’s Pro Display XDR, which offers unmatched HDR brightness and contrast alongside its impeccable build quality. There’s a big problem with these alternatives, though: They’re outrageously expensive. The Dell U3224KB is currently $2,800 and the Apple Pro Display XDR starts at $5,000. Most people who want 6K resolution will be better off buying the PA32QCV and keeping the extra cash in their wallet. Viewsonic ColorPro VP16 OLED – Best portable monitor - Numerous image quality customization options - Top-tier image quality even at default settings Who should buy the Viewsonic VP16-OLED? If you want a monitor that you can easily transport for content creation work, the Viewsonic VP16-OLED will fill that role with aplomb. This impressive monitor combines a class-leading image quality with a unique and useful stand. The VP16-OLED has a 15.6-inch OLED panel with 1080p resolution. It delivers outstanding image quality, scoring top marks in color accuracy, gamut, and contrast. The VP16-OLED’s performance is superior to many full-sized OLED monitors—and completely smashes portable competitors. This makes the VP16-OLED ideal for photographers, videographers, and other content creators. The monitor has a versatile stand. It can be used as a kickstand, as is true of most portable monitors, or expand to hold the monitor upright. The stand includes two USB-C ports, either of which can be used to provide power and video input to the monitor. It also offers a micro-HDMI port for use with devices that lack USB-C. Viewsonic VP16-OLED: Further considerations Viewsonic bundles the monitor with several cable types and a USB-C power brick, so you don’t have to buy additional adapter cables or accessories. There’s just one problem: It’s expensive. The Viewsonic VP16-OLED retails at $399.99, more than double the price of a basic 1080p portable monitor. That’s tough to justify if you just need a second monitor to display Slack and Twitter, but it’s a worthwhile upgrade if you care about image quality. - 28-inch panel with 3840×2560 resolution Who should buy the BenQ RD280U? The BenQ RD280U is the best monitor for coders thanks to its unusual 3:2 aspect ratio, which is much taller than a conventional widescreen. The extra height is great for viewing more lines of code simultaneously and reduces the need for constant scrolling back or forth. Beyond its unique aspect ratio, the RD280U’s image quality is ideal for long coding sessions. The monitor’s IPS panel delivers excellent color accuracy and wide viewing angles, ensuring code remains clear and legible from any position. The 28-inch display panel has a crisp 3840×2560 resolution, which helps to render small fonts. It also has a matte finish that reduces glare, making it ideal for various lighting conditions. The monitor has a MoonHalo ambient light and an automatic night mode, both designed to reduce eye strain during extended use — a crucial consideration for programmers who often work long hours. Connectivity is another strong suit of the RD280U, with a versatile array of ports including USB-C with DisplayPort Alternate Mode and 90 watts of USB Power Delivery. Programmers can easily connect and charge a laptop. Priced at $599.99, the BenQ RD280U is relatively expensive for a monitor of its size, but its long list of unique features makes it an easy recommendation for coders. The added cost is justified by the fact no competitor offers the same features at any price. - Alienware AW3426DW: Combines just-the-basics design with an excellent five-layer tandem QD-OLED panel to deliver great image quality at an affordable price. - Arzopa Z1FC: A budget portable monitor that can game - Alienware AW3425DW: Forgoes extra features to deliver stellar SDR and HDR image quality at an aggressive price - MSI Modern MD272UPSW: A solid smart TV powered by Google TV OS - Asus ProArt PA32UCDM: Delivers pro-worthy OLED image quality and high refresh rates, but limited connectivity holds it back Our monitor guides are based on testing by freelance and staff contributors with decades of combined experience. While we rely on our eyes for an initial impression, we thoroughly test each monitor with a Datacolor Spyder X2 Ultra color calibration tool. This specialized hardware can objectively measure a monitor’s brightness, contrast, color gamut, color accuracy, luminance and color uniformity, gamma, and many other aspects of image quality. Using this tool helps us detect strengths and weaknesses that don’t stand out at a glance and guarantees that a change in lighting conditions or monitor location won’t skew our impression. For more details, see our article on on how we test monitors at PCWorld. Who curated this article? Matthew S. Smith is a freelance technology journalist with 15 years of experience reviewing consumer electronics, including the universe of computer monitors. In addition to PCWorld, his work can be found on Wired, Digital Trends, Reviewed, Lifewire, and other technology publications. There are literally hundreds—and perhaps thousands—of monitors to choose from. Choosing one from the crowd can be difficult, but knowing the key traits of a monitor will help you make your decision. Most monitors are available in 4K (3840×2160), 1440p (2560×1440), and 1080p (1920×1080) resolution. A higher resolution provides a sharper, more attractive image and is generally preferable. There’s nothing wrong with 1080p, however. It remains the baseline and is by far the most popular resolution sold today. Look for a monitor with a connection supported by your computer. HDMI and DisplayPort are the most common. USB-C is rising in popularity because it can charge connected devices, such as a laptop. Most monitors have a 60Hz refresh rate, but a higher refresh rate (such as 144Hz) will make motion look smooth and crisp. This is most appealing to PC gamers, as improved motion performance is most noticeable when panning the camera in a 3D game. This technology also improves motion performance. It does so by keeping a monitor’s refresh rate in sync with the video input from your computer. Our guide to FreeSync and G-Sync provides more detail. Many 4K monitors support HDR, but often the HDR performance is lackluster. The HDR will function, and may look superior to SDR, but it won’t approach the quality implied by the spec. To ensure a quality HDR experience, look for a minimum of VESA DisplayHDR 1000 certification (or VESA DisplayHDR True Black). See our article on everything you need to know about HDR on your PC to learn more. Want to know more before you make a decision? Our monitor buying guide explains the nerdy details of monitor specifications. What is the best monitor? The best monitor overall is the Dell Ultrasharp U2724DE. This 27-inch IPS display with 2560×1440 resolution, a 120Hz refresh rate, and extensive connectivity options can truly do it all, from productivity to gaming. It’s solidly built, has ergonomic adjustments, and top-of-its class image quality. What is the best cheap monitor? There are monitors that are cheaper than the Acer Vero B247Y G, but none that are nearly as good for the price. Hovering around $150, the 24-inch, 1080p B247Y G exceeds its price range with a 120Hz refresh rate, adaptive sync, a fully adjustable stand, and above-average image quality. A truly great value! What size of monitor should I buy? Monitor size depends on personal preference and location. A 24-inch monitor is fine for a desk that is around 24 inches deep, or less. Its small size will still be sufficient because the monitor is closer to you. Most people, however, will want to go with a 27-inch monitor. The added size will make the monitor easy to see. This also opens up a wider range of 4K monitor options, as 4K is very rare on a 24-inch monitor. Larger monitors, such as a 32-inch widescreen or 34-inch ultrawide, are great for deep desks and people who want an immersive experience. Monitors this large can serve as a TV replacement in a small room. Displays of even larger size, such as 42-inch or 48-inch HDTVs, are best for home theater setups or an unusually large office. You’ll want to sit four to six feet away from a display of this size. What display input is best? (HDMI vs. DisplayPort vs. USB-C) USB-C is the best display input for most people. It works by bundling DisplayPort into USB-C, so offers all the same features as DisplayPort. Yet it retains the features of USB-C including optional support for Power Delivery to charge external devices. This is why we recommend a USB-C monitor for most people. DisplayPort is generally second-best. It supports higher resolutions and refresh rates than HDMI. This input is particularly common on desktop computers. HDMI comes in third due to lower resolution and refresh rate support. This is improved by HDMI 2.1, but this feature remains hard to find and often adds to a monitor’s price. All three of the options above handle 1080p at 60Hz, which is the most common resolution and refresh rate available today. It’s also important to buy a monitor that has an input compatible with your PC. Are all monitors compatible with Windows and MacOS? Modern monitors are compatible with all recent versions of Windows and MacOS. They’re plug-and-play, which means the monitor should display an image without the need to install driver software or mess with Windows or MacOS settings.

Travel editors at Condé Nast Traveler have compiled a list of the 27 Best Places to Go in 2027, reflecting current travel trends and emerging experiences. The guide highlights destinations that balance cultural significance, natural beauty, and evolving urban landscapes. Luxor, Egypt, remains a key destination, serving as a gateway to new Nile cruises set to coincide with the 'eclipse of the century' in August 2027, a follow-up to last year’s celestial event. Meanwhile, Shanghai’s transformation underscores its dual focus on business and leisure, with the Shanghai Biennale in November celebrating new gallery openings in West Bund, adjacent to the Snøhetta-designed Shanghai Grand Opera House. Jamaica, still recovering from Hurricane Melissa—the strongest to ever hit the country—one year after the storm, is welcoming travelers to participate in its rebuilding efforts, illustrating the impact of tourism on recovery. The guide also emphasizes slower, more meaningful travel, such as hiking new routes in Armenia or sailing the Cook Islands’ scenic waters. A growing preference for authentic culinary experiences over late-night restaurant reservations is noted, with a focus on traditional, earth-based meals. To escape crowded European summers, cooler climes like Denmark’s northern riviera and off-season ice trekking in Argentine Patagonia are gaining appeal. Albania’s northern Alpine region, with its snow-dipped peaks and turquoise rivers, offers a unique blend of untamed wilderness and peaceful retreats. Albanian-owned wooden B&Bs provide home-cooked meals after inn-to-inn hikes, while the area’s historical isolation during the communist era—due to its border location with Montenegro and Kosovo—has preserved its secluded charm. Abandoned bunkers from that period are a reminder of its past. Travelers are encouraged to visit before the region becomes widely known, as the feeling persists that it remains a secret to be discovered. The guide also notes the appeal of Albania’s Adriatic beaches, though the northern landscapes offer a distinct, less-commercialized experience. These 27 destinations, spanning from celestial events to cultural festivals and natural escapes, reflect a global shift toward meaningful, immersive travel experiences.
